items.title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
items.summary: The authors use honeypot services they call shibboleth traps to draw out identifying behaviour from agentic attackers, such as model declarations and writing style. They also probe harness behaviours, including how secrets are masked in tool output, command time limits and tool call scheduling. Combining these signals identifies 15 candidate models with about 90% top-1 accuracy and the correct harness with 92% accuracy, even when attackers try to conceal their identity.
items.takeaway: Attacker tooling leaves fingerprints in how it handles timeouts, secrets and scheduling, so defenders can attribute agentic intrusions by observing behaviour rather than trusting self-declared identity.

items.title: Detecting Shadow AI: Unsanctioned LLM Agents on Enterprise Endpoints: A Taxonomy, an Open Detector and a Controlled Evaluation
items.summary: The authors argue that autonomous agents will accelerate shadow IT, because agents build unsanctioned scripts, automations and MCP servers that compound faster than they are retired. They propose a taxonomy of nine agent classes and six endpoint footprint layers, and show that structural process and connection rules cannot separate an agent from a benign program talking to the same kind of service. Their open Windows detector, Agent Detector, anchors on the identity of the remote LLM service and correlates it with installation and execution history, and it flagged none of the benign twins whil
items.takeaway: Behavioural similarity can defeat rules based on process and network structure, so anchor detections on the identity of the remote service and add host history such as installation and execution records.

items.title: Treating the Model as an Untrusted Component: Deterministic Policy Enforcement, Human Approval and Taint Tracking Against Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Agents, with Validation on Open-Weights Models
items.summary: The authors compare in-prompt defences against prompt injection in tool-using agents with deterministic reference monitors, human approval and taint tracking, using open-weights Qwen2.5 models on 13 tasks and 12 tools. Real-model results show that a task-bound monitor admits very few attack calls compared with prompt guardrails, which were inconsistent across models. Simulated results suggest guardrail stacks fail under persistent adaptive attackers while the monitor holds severe actions at 0.0%, though human-approval and taint findings are simulation-only.
items.takeaway: Do not rely on the model to refuse injected instructions. Enforce what tool calls are permitted outside the model with deterministic, task-bound policies, and budget any human approval steps so they cannot be spammed.

items.title: On the Relative Security of Prompt Injection: Mechanised Definitions, Defences and Verdicts for LLM Agents
items.summary: The authors argue that noninterference is too strict for LLM agents that must read untrusted content and sometimes disclose data by design. They define relative security as requiring that every leak an agent has is also a leak a reference agent running the same plan under the same monitor already has. They introduce PlanTERS, a small agent language with a formal model, and prove in Isabelle/HOL that revoking injectable tools at the first untrusted read makes plans relatively secure under stated assumptions.
items.takeaway: Measure prompt injection risk against a reference baseline of what the plan already leaks, rather than demanding that the agent leak nothing at all.

items.title: Keel: A Verified In-Kernel Proof Checker for Proof Carrying BPF
items.summary: While formalising the in-kernel proof checker of BCF, the authors found 13 bugs, including unsound rewrite rules, unchecked proof steps and memory safety errors, and showed that forged certificates could make the kernel accept unsafe eBPF programs. They then built Keel, a checker specified in Lean, proven sound, and implemented in a verified C fragment with linear time and memory bounds. Keel is also faster than the BCF checker in the kernel, by 1.3X overall and 2.0X on the slowest certificates.
items.takeaway: Proof-carrying systems move trust into the checker, so a small in-kernel verifier is a high-value attack surface and is worth formal verification alongside the verifier it supports.

items.title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
items.summary: This systematisation of knowledge screens 98 sources and codes 284 distinct attacks against agentic AI systems, along with 452 safeguards and 660 attack to safeguard relationships. Tool, MCP and action-layer attacks make up the largest share, while prompt injection and action hijacking have the broadest coverage. Only 278 of the 660 relationships are directly assessed, which shows that defensive evidence is thin.
items.takeaway: Threat models for agents should track when an attack is inserted versus when it activates, because many agent attacks persist silently before they trigger.

items.title: StealthyPoison: Manipulating LLM Agent Behavior through Procedural Poisoning of Third-Party Skills
items.summary: StealthyPoison corrupts the decision-critical rules inside a third-party agent skill while keeping its advertised function intact, so overtly malicious text is avoided. The attack builds reusable poisoned procedures using a surrogate agent, then boosts retrieval metadata so the poisoned skill is selected over benign alternatives. It improves top-1 poisoned placement by 13.6% over HotFlip and GCG, and most payloads evade SkillSpector and GPT-5.4-mini.
items.takeaway: Supply chain risk for agents sits in the procedures they follow, not just the code they run, so skills from public registries need the same review as other third-party dependencies.

items.title: Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents
items.summary: WebTrap Farm is an evaluation framework that tests web agents against malicious user prompts, prompt injection and deceptive web design across four harness stages. Existing harnesses were vulnerable to typical attacks, and some unsafe behaviour occurred without any explicit attack content. Both the harness and the backend model significantly affected security outcomes, so the authors argue the harness itself is a security boundary that needs its own design controls.
items.takeaway: When assessing an agent, test the harness that interprets pages and turns model output into browser actions as well as the model, because harness design alone can create injection-driven failures.

items.title: Scaling Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks with Agent Swarms
items.summary: The authors build a synthetic prompt injection dataset that uses benign actions as adversarial goals, which isolates instruction-hierarchy compliance from security knowledge. An agentic attacker with greater capabilities reliably gets several frontier models to follow instructions embedded in tool output, including models that did well on public benchmarks. They argue that defences need proactive, automated red teaming to keep pace.
items.takeaway: Static benchmark scores can overstate robustness, so run adaptive, automated attackers against agent tool outputs to find failures that fixed payloads miss.

items.title: PRISM: Causal Counterfactual Minimization of Agent Tool Privileges via Information Bottleneck Role Induction
items.summary: The paper applies role engineering to LLM agents rather than human users, aiming to cut the over-authorisation that occurs when an agent receives every tool exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). PRISM tests whether each tool is causally necessary by intervening in a sandbox, compresses agent trajectories with an information bottleneck, and picks the number of roles from the knee of the rate-distortion curve. On AgentDojo, τ-bench and ToolEmu, it reports a 78.3% reduction in authorised tools per role, a 78.2% task success rate and a 15.9% blast radius.
items.takeaway: Least privilege for agents should be decided by testing which tools a task actually needs, not by granting the full tool catalogue by default.

items.title: EVAX: Towards a Practical, Pro-active & Adaptive Architecture for High Performance & Security
items.summary: The authors propose EVAX, a framework that trains ML detectors and adds security-focused performance counters to spot microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre, LVI and Rowhammer, including evasive and zero-day variants. Mitigations are switched on only when an attack is detected, cutting InvisiSpec overhead to 1.26% and Fencing overhead to 3.45%. The detector reports about 4 false positives per million instructions in their experiments.
items.takeaway: Always-on hardware mitigations are often too costly to deploy, so detect-then-mitigate designs can make strong defences practical if the detector is hard to evade and produces few false positives.

items.title: MicroSim: Contrastive Graph Neural Networks for Binary Code Similarity Detection
items.summary: MicroSim represents functions as graphs built from IDA Hex-Rays microcode and compares them with a contrastive Siamese graph neural network for binary code similarity. Under a strict split that prevents function leakage between training and test, it outperforms Gemini, SAFE, jTrans and a bag-of-words baseline on the TREX cross-optimisation benchmark. The authors also analyse why pair classification scores do not carry over to ranked retrieval, showing a low mean reciprocal rank even when classification is strong.
items.takeaway: A high pairwise ROC-AUC does not mean a similarity model will rank the right match first in a search, so evaluate retrieval metrics such as MRR and recall at k separately for binary analysis tools.

items.title: Coding Agents Propagate Vulnerabilities in Code Bases
items.summary: The study shows that coding agents copy vulnerable patterns from existing code, reducing the share of secure backend implementations by 3.4% on average. In real C and C++ repositories, the gap between secure and insecure contexts reaches 35.4%. Security prompts did not stop the propagation, and agents often justified the flawed code by pointing to existing code, even though they recognised the vulnerability in 69.9% of cases.
items.takeaway: Existing insecure code acts as a template for generated code, so fixing vulnerabilities at the source is needed to stop them spreading as agents write more of the codebase.

items.title: Least-Privilege Auditing of Agent Tool Calls with Intent Graphs and Reasoning-Guided Escalation
items.summary: The authors propose a runtime audit for tool-calling agents that derives an intent graph from the user's objective and tool catalogue with a single LLM call per task. A deterministic checker then validates each tool call against that graph with no further LLM calls, at a median of 5.7 microseconds per call. Flagged calls are escalated to a reasoning guardian that sees only the objective, plan and flagged call, and lookups of the user's own state skip the audit because the harm lies in writes or outward actions. The authors note that end-to-end validation remains open because the current agent
items.takeaway: Put the expensive reasoning on the rare suspicious actions and keep a cheap deterministic check on everything else, and focus audits on writes and outward steps where harm occurs.

items.title: ErosionBench: Probing Alignment Decay in Enterprise Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: ErosionBench tests whether benign-looking requests in enterprise multi-agent systems can gradually escalate into unsafe tool calls through shared state and trusted peer messages. It scores the realised tool action against authorised intent rather than output text, across 1,728 scenarios and 198 image-based attacks. Perimeter defences often reduce attacks by over-refusing 54 to 92% of legitimate work, while the proposed trajectory-based Meta-Auditor reaches 98.5% recall at a 2.9% false positive rate.
items.takeaway: A low attack success rate can hide heavy over-refusal, so measure defences on both blocked attacks and the legitimate work they stop, and monitor the actions an agent takes rather than the text it produces.
